faq.q: Why does the stomach contain air in many EA cases?

faq.a: Yes, polyhydramnios and absent stomach bubble on ultrasound raise suspicion, but definitive diagnosis is post‑natal.
Survival exceeds 90 % in high‑resource settings; in low‑resource hospitals, outcomes depend on timely surgery and management of associated anomalies.

exam: What bedside maneuver confirms suspicion of esophageal atresia? — Attempt NG tube insertion; coiling at 10–12 cm suggests a blind pouch.
How does a chest X‑ray differentiate isolated EA from EA with distal TEF? — Presence of air in the stomach indicates a distal fistula.
A newborn with EA presents with severe respiratory distress after feeding. What is your first emergency step? — Place infant prone, suction oral secretions, and keep airway clear.
Why is a long‑gap EA not repaired in the first 24 hours? — The gap is too large for tension‑free anastomosis; staged repair reduces leak risk.
Which associated anomaly most influences peri‑operative planning? — Cardiac defects; they affect anaesthetic risk and may require pre‑operative cardiology input.
What postoperative complication should you monitor for in the first week? — Anastomotic leak presenting with tachypnea, fever, or increased chest drainage.
Why are water‑soluble contrast agents preferred for the contrast study? — They are less irritating if aspirated, reducing risk of chemical pneumonitis.

In a low‑resource setting without fluoroscopy, how can you assess the gap length? — Measure the distance between the upper pouch and lower esophageal segment intra‑operatively or use a calibrated NG tube.
ai.title: Esophageal Atresia
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Congenital interruption of the esophagus, often with a tracheoesophageal fistula, presents with feeding difficulty and respiratory distress. Prompt recognition and surgical repair are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Incidence ~1 in 3,500 live births
More common in males
Associated anomalies: VACTERL, cardiac defects, renal anomalies
sections.p: Esophageal atresia (EA) is a birth defect where the esophagus ends in a blind pouch; 85% have a distal tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF). It blocks oral feeding and can cause aspiration.

b: Type C: blind upper pouch, fistula from lower segment to trachea
Long‑gap EA: >3 cm or >2 vertebral bodies, often needs staged repair
Associated anomalies raise peri‑operative risk
sections.p: EA is classified by the Gross (or Vogt) system; the most frequent type is Type C (proximal EA + distal TEF). Severity is judged by the length of the gap and associated anomalies.

b: Failed NG tube passage – key bedside clue
Respiratory distress after feeds – suggests aspiration via TEF
Abdominal distension – gas from fistula
sections.p: Newborns cannot pass a nasogastric tube beyond 10–12 cm and develop frothy saliva, coughing, cyanosis with feeds, and a scaphoid abdomen.

t.b: Confirms tube coiling in upper pouch and presence of air in stomach (sign of distal TEF)
Defines length of gap and fistula location
Detects associated cardiac defects that affect anaesthesia

b: Position infant prone, keep head low, suction saliva frequently
IV fluids and electrolytes; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics if sepsis suspected
Primary repair: right posterolateral thoracotomy, ligate TEF, anastomose esophageal ends
Long‑gap: delayed primary anastomosis, gastric pull‑up, or colon interposition
Avoid nasogastric feeds until repair; use transpyloric feeding if needed
sections.p: Stabilise airway, prevent aspiration, and arrange definitive surgical repair (usually within 2–3 days).

b: Forgetting to check NG tube length – may miss blind pouch
Using contrast media with high osmolarity – risk of aspiration pneumonitis
Neglecting associated anomalies – can cause peri‑operative mortality
sections.p: Errors often stem from assuming a normal NG tube passage, delaying suction, or attempting oral feeds before repair.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent cyanosis or apnea after feeds
